paper_title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Visual agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) have made rapid progress on computer-use and embodied tasks [25, 37, 43, 53, 67]. Video games pose broader challenge for visual intelligence [28, 39, 46, 47, 52, 58]: each game brings its own visuals, rules and controls, which an agent must infer from the screen while reasoning over changing scene and acting with precise timing. This diversity makes gameplay experience valuable source of training data for general-purpose visual agents. We therefore aim to collect gameplay data at scale across diverse games for visual agent training. Equal contribution. Project lead. Emails: xiruij@illinois.edu, ry21@illinois.edu 1 Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through EnvironmentPlayer Co-Development central bottleneck is obtaining such gameplay experience at scale: learning requires trajectories that pair actions with explicit goals and reliable signals of success. Human gameplay recordings [16, 19, 23, 34, 80] are expensive to collect, and online gameplay videos lack actions, which have to be recovered with inverse-dynamics or latent-action models [2, 9, 41, 73]; in both cases, goals and outcomes are annotated after the fact [3, 39, 56, 74]. Interactive game environments provide all three natively [1, 20, 27, 30, 32, 33, 77, 79], but each new game demands game-specific engineering, which limits their coverage. Coding agents could automate both the environment building and gameplay needed for data collection. They can synthesize verifiable environments from code repositories and websites [5, 51, 60, 66], write games from scratch [36, 72], and develop executable policies for playing games [52]. Adapting existing web games for such data collection requires locating their internal state in engine-specific code and using it to define task initialization, progress measures and success checks. However, the resulting environment may pass the coding agents own tests even when task is impossible to complete, its progress measure fails to update, or its success check triggers too early. Such defects may only become apparent when an agent actually plays the task. This motivates environmentplayer co-development: environments and the players that test them are developed together, each improving the other through play. Building on this principle, we present Game2Player, framework in which Builder agent and two players, VLM Player and Coding Player, co-develop verifiable environments from in-the-wild web games  (Fig. 2)  . The Builder sets up each game in sandboxed, reproducible runtime, exposes its internal state, and defines tasks whose progress and success are read from that state, guided by engine-specific skills. The players then attempt every task: the VLM Player plays from screenshots, pausing the game while it reasons, whereas the Coding Player writes Python policy over player-visible state, runs it in real time and refines the code from the recorded outcomes. When failure traces back to the environment, the players report it, either as defect, such as key with no effect or progress that never moves, or as request for on-screen information that the policy cannot read. The Builder checks each report against the recorded episode before repairing the environment, and accepts an environment once the players episodes confirm its own evaluation (Sec. 3.2). Once an environment is accepted, the players turn from testing it to collecting experience in it, and every recorded episode is paired with its task instruction and dense, state-based progress signal. The two players are complementary teachers, offering efficient demonstration collection and visually grounded action explanations, respectively. code policy can be rerun without any model calls, supplying high-quality demonstrations quickly and at scale. The VLM Player acts on the same screenshots that the trained agent will see and explains each action in short note, so its episodes show how to approach game even when they fall short of the goal. We distill both sources into one pixel-based agent with progress-weighted SFT, which up-weights actions that advance task progress. Using Game2Player, we have built 568 verified environments with 3,436 tasks across more than 25 genres and seven engines. As verifiable game benchmarks remain limited in both number and diversity, we also use it to construct PlayerBench, 50 held-out games with 287 tasks for evaluating game agents on unseen games. In controlled rebuild of 20 games, player reports raise the share of correctly implemented tasks from 65% to 72% and the tasks solved by code policies from 34 to 46. The code policies written in the loop play in real time without model calls and record 22 times as many steps per hour as VLM Player. Training on 15.7K trajectories more than doubles the PlayerBench progress of Qwen3.5-9B, from 14.3% to 31.2%, and the gains transfer to the external benchmark GameWorld [30], where Game2Player-9B reaches 53.1%, higher than the published results of several proprietary models. Beyond these results, our ablations examine how progress-weighted SFT, the data from each player, and thinking at inference time contribute to the gains. In summary, our contributions are: Environmentplayer co-development: Game2Player, scalable framework where Builder and two players use gameplay feedback to build and validate verifiable environments; 2 Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through EnvironmentPlayer Co-Development PlayerBench: 50 held-out games and 287 tasks, more challenging than GameWorld, where agents of Tab. 3 score on average 12.8 and 7.6 points lower progress and success; Progress-weighted distillation: training on 15.7K trajectories from both players more than doubles Qwen3.5-9Bs progress on PlayerBench, with gains transferring to GameWorld.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Interactive game benchmarks. Existing game benchmarks span text and grid games [14, 32, 61], puzzles and adventures [1, 11], browser games [20, 30, 48], and commercial or 3D environments [27, 46, 77]. GameWorld [30] provides state-based verification for 34 browser games; AI GameStore [72] generates 100 games with human involvement; and PlaySuite [50] evaluates thousands of open-source games with video-language judge. Game2Player automates the adaptation of existing games into state-verified environments for both training and evaluation. Offline game benchmarks and gameplay data. Question-answering benchmarks on gameplay video [4, 29, 44, 45, 56, 57] test perception without play, and strong offline scores do not imply strong play [56, 64]. Gameplay corpora with recorded or inferred actions train generalist game agents [2, 9, 26, 28, 58, 73], and some add language annotations afterwards [3, 39, 56]. Synthetic games with verifiable rewards improve VLM reasoning [7, 49, 62]. Our trajectories are collected against task, so every step carries its instruction, its state-grounded progress and its outcome. Tab. 1 compares Game2Player with game benchmarks and gameplay datasets. Environment synthesis for agents. Automated pipelines construct verifiable environments from code repositories [22, 66], terminal tasks [15, 42], websites and applications [5, 51, 60], or recreate games from observation [36]. Open-ended learning further co-evolves environments and agents [12, 13, 54, 75]. In Game2Player, the feedback that drives repairs comes from two players with different views who play every task of an existing game, and the Builder checks their failures against the recordings before repairing the environment. We apply co-development to refine the environments while developing two complementary players for scalable data collection. Training visual agents. Visual agents learn from trajectories through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning across embodied, computer-use and game environments [6, 8, 28, 55, 63, 68, 69]. Concurrent work scales gameplay training: PLAYER-1 [31] uses demonstrations from 172 games followed by RL in 16 synthetic environments, while GameScaling [78] continues pre-training on up to 1,600 hours of gameplay. We instead collect complementary demonstrations from code policies and visual player in verified environments and distill them through progress-weighted SFT, achieving higher progress and success rates on both PlayerBench and GameWorld. Code policies, privileged teachers and reasoning. Code can serve directly as game agents policy [52, 65]. Distilling teacher with privileged information into student that sees less is long-standing recipe in embodied learning [10, 35, 59]. We use state-reading code policies as teachers for pixel-based students and weight their supervision by measured task progress, related in spirit to step-level filtering of agent trajectories [18]. Our weights come from progress events measured in the game state, and they set how often each step is sampled. Reasoning in agent trajectories is either produced by the agent itself [37, 58, 71], written afterwards [55, 63, 70], or grounded in privileged state [10, 21, 76]. Game2Player follows the first route, retaining the VLM Players own notes and native thinking during play as supervision, whereas code policy demonstrations carry neither kind of text and supervise actions only.

sections.title: 3.1 Environments, tasks and players
sections.content: We model game as partially observed process with hidden state st, keyboard and mouse actions at and screenshots ot. verifiable environment wraps the game so that it runs offline from fixed seed and pauses while model chooses an action. Through one interface, the state API, it exposes two views of st. The state probe ϕ(st) is small set of named variables read from the running game, such as the players health, and only scoring reads it. The player observation ψ(st), which code policies read, holds named fields, such as the positions of visible objects, limited to what person could see or infer from the screen, with no hidden information such as face-down cards.

sections.title: 3.3 Gameplay data from two players
sections.content: Both players record training gameplay in the accepted environments, and their data are complementary. code policy calls no model while it plays, so it can be rerun from new seeds at little cost, whereas VLM Player episodes keep the models notes and thinking and also cover tasks that no code policy completes. To train on both, we bring them into one format. VLM Player episodes already follow the harness, one action per step. code policy acts continuously, so we cut its recording into harness steps (Fig. 3, middle): the recorder logs every key press and release with its time, and we convert this log into harness actions. In total, the two players recorded 15.7K trajectories with 307 hours of gameplay, with more details in Tab. 8. Of the resulting 1.56M training examples, code policies provide 87.7% and VLM Players 12.3%.

sections.title: 3.4 Progress-weighted SFT
sections.content: A trajectory spends long stretches waiting, wandering or recovering from mistakes, while only few actions, such as well-timed jump or the turn into portal, move the task forward. The progress pt recorded in every trajectory (Eq. (2)) tells these actions apart, and progress-weighted SFT uses it to weight the training examples. Each example pairs the harness context xt at step t, the same input that the trained model receives when it plays, with target yt: the action at for code policy step, and the action together with the note and thinking, when present, for VLM Player step. Its weight is wt ρt max(1, ct), (3) where the credit ct raises the weight of the last few actions before each rise in progress or success, since these actions most likely caused it, and the penalty ρt removes or lowers the weight of the final actions of failed and timed-out episodes and of repeated actions that do not improve progress. The weights of games with many examples are also scaled down, so that few long games do not dominate. Fig. 5 illustrates these rules, and Tab. 11 gives their exact values and time windows. sections.title: 4.1 Benchmarks and setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. We split the Game2Player collection by game and hold out 50 games with all 287 of their tasks as PlayerBench, so no trajectory from PlayerBench game is used for training. PlayerBench covers seven engines and four difficulty tiers (App. D). We also evaluate on GameWorld [30], an independently built benchmark of 34 browser games and 170 tasks with state-based scoring and no overlap with our collection. We evaluate GameWorld with our harness rather than its generalist one; neither is consistently better (Tab. 14). On both, we report Progress, the mean episode score over equally weighted games, and Success, the share of tasks completed. Protocol. VLM Player attempts each task once from the same seed, playing through the harness at temperature 1 for at most 100 steps while the game pauses for each decision. Our trained models and the open-weight baselines see 50 steps of text history and six earlier screenshots besides the current one, while API models receive their full text history. Each step may use at most 512 output tokens with thinking off and 32,768 with thinking on. Training. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B [38] with progress-weighted SFT on our gameplay data, keeping the vision encoder frozen, which gives Game2Player-4B and Game2Player-9B. Both sizes share one recipe: one epoch of 9,237 steps at learning rate 105 with cosine decay. sections.title: 4.2 Co-development builds correct and solvable environments
sections.content: Setup. We measure what the co-development loop adds by building the same 20 games with 145 frozen tasks in three settings (App. E). The full loop runs Game2Player with GPT-6.1 Terra Builder and GPT-6.1 Sol players, and reports return to the Builder for up to two rounds of repair. The no-reports setting shares the build and play of the full loop up to the first report, after which the environment stays as delivered and the Coding Player continues with the same budget. The generic-agent setting gives the same games and task requests to generic coding agent with the Builders model but without our skills and tools, and second generic agent writes the code policy. An auditor model checks every task against the original game and the frozen task definition, and we verify its verdicts by hand. tasks environment is correct when it runs the original game and implements the tasks start, progress and success faithfully, and task is solved when its environment is correct and the final code policy completes it from two seeds. Results. Fig. 6 splits the 145 tasks of each setting into solved, correct but unsolved, and incorrect. The generic agent leaves 120 environments incorrect and solves one task, so the same model without our skills, tools and players cannot build faithful environments. With our Builder, player reports cut the incorrect environments from 51 to 40 and raise the solved tasks from 34 to 46. They work in two ways: defect reports expose bugs that the Builders own tests missed, and observation requests give the Coding Player state that it cannot read itself (Tab. 2). In There Is No Game, for example, the Coding Player reported that progress stopped at 0.9, and after the repair all nine tasks are correct and solved, while without reports all nine remain wrong. With GPT-6.1 Sol as the Builder, the full loop and the no-reports setting both give 136 correct environments, and reports still raise the solved tasks from 62 to 82. Cost. Reports add 20% to the model cost per game, from $17.7 to $21.3. Recording gameplay then costs the two players differently in kind  (Fig. 7)  . sections.title: 4.4 Ablations and analysis
sections.content: Tab. 4 and Fig. 10 vary the data source, the sampling weights, the amount of data and the number of training steps for both model sizes. We run all ablations with thinking off, which substantially reduces inference cost and allows broader set of comparisons. Data source. Each kind of player improves the base models on its own, and the two help in different ways. On PlayerBench, VLM Player data is far more sample-efficient: with 0.19M examples it raises the 4B model from 12.7% to 25.1% progress, against 17.3% for 1.37M code policy examples, since it matches the evaluation format, with paused steps from screenshots, and keeps the models notes and any native thinking. On GameWorld, code policy data alone gives the best model at both sizes, with 12 Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through EnvironmentPlayer Co-Development Figure 11 Qwen3.5-4B and Game2Player-4B on four held-out PlayerBench tasks, with thinking on and at most 100 steps. Each panel shows the final frame of each model with its final progress, and the best progress reached after each step. 36.8% and 38.0% progress, likely because its precisely timed key presses and holds transfer to games outside our collection. Combining both sources gives the best 9B model on PlayerBench, with 28.6% against 25.6% and 20.1% for single sources, while the 4B combination falls between them. Progress weighting. At an equal number of examples, progress-weighted SFT outperforms uniform sampling from the same recordings for both model sizes and on both benchmarks. It raises PlayerBench progress from 20.9% to 23.4% for the 4B model and from 23.9% to 28.6% for the 9B model, and GameWorld progress from 33.5% to 34.9% and from 31.1% to 33.9%. Its credits, penalties and game balancing (Sec. 3.4) focus training on the few actions that move task forward. Data volume and training steps. More training data keeps helping (Fig. 10, left): even 100K examples improve on the base models, and growing to all 1.56M raises PlayerBench progress from 21.2% to 23.4% for 4B and from 21.2% to 28.6% for 9B. Over training steps, PlayerBench progress keeps rising until the final checkpoint, while GameWorld progress plateaus after about 3K steps (Fig. 10, right).

sections.title: 4.5 Case studies on held-out tasks
sections.content: An important behavior that training teaches is precise timing control. In the held-out platformer Give Up (Fig. 11, top left), how long the direction keys are held largely decides how far the character runs and jumps. Within 100 steps, Qwen3.5-4B reaches 12.3% progress, while Game2Player-4B reaches 92.5%. Game2Player-4B sets an explicit hold duration on 47% of its key presses, against 1% for its base model. With identical harness instructions for both models, the model learns timing control from our data, in which code policy recordings are cut into timed holds and VLM Players use holds routinely. The other three tasks in Fig. 11 come from different genres. In Alfonzos Bowling Challenge, the task is to destroy forty bricks with ball steered by the arrow keys. Qwen3.5-4B sets hold duration on 2 of its 98 key presses, alternates between left and right, and destroys two bricks. Game2Player-4B sets duration on 69 of its 71 key presses, waits on 29 steps to follow the ball and destroys 39 bricks within 100 steps. In Kingdom Rush, the task is to build four towers. Qwen3.5-4B clicks and presses keys for 100 steps without building tower, and 11 of its steps are invalid. Game2Player-4B opens the build menu on grass tiles beside the road, waits for gold when it cannot pay for the next tower, and builds the fourth tower at step 56. In the card game Forward, the knight moves by being dragged onto an adjacent card. Qwen3.5-4B mixes 34 clicks with 58 drags, and its progress stops at 20% after step 23. 13 Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through EnvironmentPlayer Co-Development Game2Player-4B drags the knight from card to card and clears the area in 78 steps. Before some of its moves it hovers over card to read it. Fig. 23 in App. adds the task instructions and the initial frames.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Game2Player is scalable pipeline that co-develops verifiable game environments with the players that use them, whose reports catch defects the Builders own tests miss. The same loop scales up gameplay experience through cheap code policy reruns and VLM Player episodes that keep notes and thinking. Distilled with progress-weighted SFT, this experience roughly doubles the PlayerBench progress of Qwen3.5 models and transfers to GameWorld. Limitations. Accepted environments are not guaranteed to be correct. An environment is accepted once it passes the Builders evaluation, the scripted gate and the players reports, without full human audit. The audit of the co-development study finds that 72% of the tasks built by the GPT-6.1 Terra Builder and 94% of those built by the GPT-6.1 Sol Builder are implemented correctly, and human review of all 287 PlayerBench tasks found no environment or scoring errors (App. F). The pipeline covers single-player web games that run offline in browser, and online, multiplayer and large commercial games add licensing and runtime constraints that we do not address. VLM Player plays with the game paused at every decision, so our scores do not measure play under real-time latency. The Builder, the players and many baselines are proprietary models whose versions change over time, so rebuilding the collection with other models may give different environments. We discuss the broader impact in App. H.

sections.title: A Environment construction
sections.content: Scout. The Scout searches game portals such as itch.io and other public source repositories. For each candidate it checks whether the game can be played alone and offline, whether its goals split into short tasks, whether it can be restarted reliably, and how its state could be read, for example from named variables in the source. It records evidence of play and the games license, and recommends to build, reserve or skip the game. Builder phases. The Builder runs four phases. Discover inspects feasibility and proposes tasks grounded in the source or in play. Implement packages the offline game and implements the state API, JavaScript module loaded with the game, the control guide, and the start routine, progress and success of every task, editing only fixed set of paths. Evaluate plays every task start from the players view, then tests real controls, state changes and task definitions without editing files. It labels each tasks start, progress and success as verified, pending or unsupported. Builder pass requires that every task still matches the frozen plan, every start is verified, no progress or success definition is unsupported, and every verified progress definition cites recorded change of its state variable. It also requires at least one state variable read from the game rather than estimated from the screen, and check from the players view that the screen shows no defect and that every control does what the control guide says. Revise diagnoses the recorded evidence of the last evaluation before applying bounded fix. The evaluation instructions state that the presence of an interface or zero exit code is not evidence and that tasks should not be solved merely to pass evaluation. Retired tasks and unsuitable games. frozen task that the game itself cannot complete, or whose start, progress or success still cannot be measured faithfully after bounded attempt, is retired with its reason and record that shows it. task that is long or hard stays in the plan. At most third of the plan may be retired. game that would need more retired tasks, or whose progress could only be estimated from the screen, is unsuitable. Engine skills. The pipeline uses 13 skills, namely the Builder skill, eight engine skills for HTML5 capture, Unity WebGL, Flash, PICO-8, GameMaker, Godot, Construct and Defold, and four policy skills for general policies, canvas user interfaces, PICO-8 and Unity. The Builder selects an engine skill from the detected engine, and the Coding Player selects the relevant policy guidance. Each skill is short instruction file with references to engine tools, and Fig. 12 shows the skill for Godot. State contract and scripted gate. The state returned by the state API contains schema version, the game identifier, wall-clock and game time, status, whether the game is actionable, terminal outcome, game-specific state block and numeric metrics. The scripted gate checks these types, an actionable start, numeric score paths for every task, the terminal outcome domain, task definitions against the frozen plan, and finite targets above their start values. For each task start it loads the game with the external network blocked and fixed seed, and then tests two resets. Coding Player procedure and acceptance. The Coding Player runs Discover, Implement, Evaluate, Diagnose and Revise. It inspects the visible information and the player observation, writes one code policy per game, records bounded headless episodes, separates policy failures from environment defects and retests after each revision. The Coding Player collects the player observation with probe that it writes for each game. Every field of the probe comes from named source, such as game object or page element, and the probe may read anything person could see on the screen but no hidden information. When visible quantity cannot be read without changing the game, the Coding Player files an observation request, and the Builder adds the quantity to the player observation. Every task needs at least two recorded attempts, and every task reported as completed needs at least two successful episodes of the current code policy. For game with > 1 tasks, code policy is accepted if it completes at least max(2, n/4 + 1) tasks, and single-task game requires that task. Reports and repair. Tab. 5 lists what each player may report. The reports of game start new Builder run, which goes through all four phases with the frozen task plan. sections.content: Prompt. The system prompt consists of fixed opening, the game rules and the role and controls written by the Builder, the task instruction and the output format, which restricts actions to the games allowed controls. Fig. 18 shows the system prompt and the user message of one step, with the parts written for each game and task replaced by placeholders. History. For the models we train and the open-weight baselines, the context contains the current screenshot and up to 50 previous steps, each with its step number, action and note. API models receive all previous steps. Only the last six historical steps carry screenshots, so request contains at most seven images. Native thinking is not inserted into the history. Action space. Each step returns one action, which may contain timed key sequence. Keyboard actions press one key, press several keys together, set held keys or play an ordered key sequence. Pointer actions click, hold, move, drag and scroll, and the vocabulary also includes typing and waiting. key press or click without duration is 0.05-second tap, and durations are capped at 10 seconds. Qwen models emit JSON tool call with pointer coordinates normalized to 01000. Budgets and failures. The step budget counts every model call, including calls without valid action. Reaching the budget without completing the task is timeout that keeps the best progress reached. Depending on the task, terminal failure ends the episode or triggers reset within the same budget. case counts as evaluated only with valid recording, usable outcome and at least 90% state coverage, and infrastructure failures are rescheduled. PlayerBench composition. PlayerBench contains 50 games and 287 tasks, with 2 to 10 tasks per game. The Builder assigns every task one of four difficulty tiers, and PlayerBench has 98 easy, 105 medium, 67 hard and 17 very hard tasks. By engine there are 12 Unity WebGL, 10 HTML5, 7 Flash, 7 Godot, 6 GameMaker, 6 PICO-8 and 2 Construct games. By genre there are 9 puzzle, 6 action, 6 platformer, 5 shooter, 4 strategy and 3 simulation games, 2 games each of adventure, card, RPG, racing, rhythm and survival, and one game each of arcade, board, fighting, sports and other genres. The study uses 20 games from the collection, spread over seven engines, with their 145 task definitions frozen, so all settings implement the same goals. In the full loop and the no-reports setting, the Builder builds each game once with its engine skills and tools. The VLM Player then plays every task and the Coding Player writes code policy until the first player report, and the run forks at that report. In the full loop, the report returns to the Builder, which checks it against the recording and repairs the environment, and the players continue on the repaired environment, for up to two rounds of repair. Each Builder run may revise its environment up to three times, the Coding Player may revise its policy up to 50 times, and the VLM Player plays each task for up to 100 steps from seed 67. In the no-reports setting, no report reaches the Builder, and the Coding Player continues on the delivered environment with the same budget. The two settings thus start from the same environment and differ only in the reports, and game without any report ends identical in both. In the generic-agent setting, generic coding agent receives the original game, the frozen task requests and the basic interface to run the game, without project skills or engine-analysis tools. second generic agent then writes code policy for the delivered environment, which it may not edit, and both agents use the Builders model. Each generic agent works in single session of up to 90 minutes and may test its own work. The final code policies of the full loop and the no-reports setting play every task from seeds 67 and 68 for up to 600 seconds, and the policy writer of the generic-agent setting records its own episodes. task is solved when its environment is correct and two of these episodes complete it. We run the study with GPT-6.1 Terra Builder and GPT-6.1 Sol players, as in Sec. 4.2, and repeat it with GPT-6.1 Sol for every agent, all at medium reasoning effort. Judging environments. One auditor session per game, GPT-6.1 Sol at high reasoning effort, compares the environments of all settings with the original game files and the frozen task requests. It traces each metric to native game state, inspects the recorded episodes and runs its own checks, and for each task it decides whether the environment runs the original game and whether its start, progress and success match the task. Humans additionally check its verdicts. Tab. 15 gives the outcome of every game in both experiments, and Fig. 21 their totals. With the Terra Builder, the reports make 11 more tasks correct and add 12 solved tasks, at 20% more model cost. Defect repairs make the environments of three games correct, and observation requests let the code policies solve tasks in three more games (Tab. 16). The generic agent builds 25 correct environments and solves one task. It replaced the original game in three games and left it unplayable in one, and in most other tasks its progress or success checks do not follow the game. With GPT-6.1 Sol as both the Builder and the players, the full loop and the no-reports setting each produce 136 correct task environments, while the number solved by the code policy rises from 62 to 82. The additional solutions come from six games where the reports lead to richer observations and clearer control guidance, allowing the code policies to solve more tasks without changing which task environments are correct. Reports and repairs. Tab. 16 lists every report of the Terra experiment and what the full loop changed. Eleven games received player reports, and two more had start failures reported by the harness. The full loop changed eleven environments, with three repairs of defects, four sets of new observations and four clarifications of the control guide, the start or the reported state. In There Is No Game, the Coding Player found that progress stopped at 0.9 after the letter had fallen, because the Builder had hooked the games events before some of their variables existed; after the repair all nine tasks are correct and solved, while without reports all nine remain wrong. This is typical of the defects that reports catch: the tasks of game share its instrumentation, so one defect breaks all of them and one repair fixes them all. Reports of the VLM Player led to two more repairs, of crash in Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers and of an upgrade menu that ran off the screen in Dome Romantik. In Where the Water Flows and Strike Force Heroes, observation requests made the Builder expose the terrain, the player and the visible enemies, and the code policies solved four tasks in each game, against none without reports. Of the 568 games in the collection, 298 have complete construction records. The Builder marked VLM Player reports as fixed in 23 games and revisited the environment after Coding Player feedback in 125 games, covering 134 games in total. Cost. sections.title: F Human play
sections.content: Protocol. Participants play PlayerBench tasks in their own desktop browser, on web page that serves the same environments as the evaluation with the same seed. They read the task instruction and the control guide, as the VLM Players do, and play in real time with keyboard and mouse, for at most 10 minutes per attempt. An attempt ends when the tasks success check fires, when the participant ends it or at the time limit, and game that allows another try after loss restarts within the attempt. The page records the video, the inputs and the state trace in the same format as the other players, and the same evaluator scores every attempt. 34 Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through EnvironmentPlayer Co-Development Figure 21 Task outcomes of all three settings in both experiments. task is solved when its environment is correct and the final code policy completes it. Participants and coverage. The study had 15 participants, recruited through our advertisements in various channels. Each participant played between 3 and 67 tasks, 19.8 on average, with 302 attempts over all 287 tasks. Alongside the performance evaluation, human review checked all 287 tasks for playability and scoring consistency. We checked whether progress reflected advancement toward the stated goal and whether the success conditions matched completion of that goal in the game. No environment or scoring errors were found. Fig. 24 summarizes the participants age and gender and the attempts of each participant. Consent and privacy. Before playing, participants were told on the study page that their gameplay video and their keyboard and mouse input would be recorded for research, and they took part voluntarily and could stop at any time. The recording covers only the game area of the shared browser tab, without audio, microphone or webcam. Participants enter name or nickname, which is stored separately from the recordings, and the age group and gender in Fig. 24 are self-reported and shown only in aggregate. Scoring. We score the first attempt of each participant at task, so that practice on the same task does not count. tasks progress and success are the means over its scored attempts, and they are then averaged over tasks and games. Different tasks are played by different participants, so the human row of Tab. 3 describes population of players who meet these games for the first time, not single expert. Humans play in real time, while models pause the game at every step, so the human scores are reference for first-time play rather than an upper bound. The human scores on GameWorld in Tab. 3 are those of the expert player reported by GameWorld [30], who had studied the game rules and practiced the controls and played each task with at most 100 primitive actions. Results. Human players reach 69.4% progress and 51.8% success on PlayerBench. sections.title: H Broader impact
sections.content: The games in our collection belong to their creators. Only small share of them come with open-source licenses, and the others are freely playable on public web portals but are not licensed for redistribution. We use them only for research and do not distribute the games, their assets or the instrumented environments, and all third-party games and assets remain subject to their owners rights and licenses. We release the source code of Game2Player, the trained models and the task specifications. Other materials remain under review pending copyright and redistribution considerations. Agents that learn to play games from screenshots could also be used to automate play in online games whose terms of service forbid bots, and our collection contains only single-player games that run offline.
